permits.name: Form your legal entity with the Florida Division of Corporations (Sunbiz)
permits.issuing_agency: Florida Department of State – Division of Corporations (Sunbiz)
permits.notes: File online: an LLC costs $125 ($100 filing + $25 registered agent designation), a for-profit corporation $70 ($35 + $35); a certified copy and certificate of status are optional extras. Annual reports are due January 1 to May 1 ($138.75 LLC / $150 corporation) and jump by $400 if filed after May 1. Do this first: the EIN, DOR registration, DBPR and alcohol applications, and the City of Miami Certificate of Use all expect the exact Sunbiz entity name, and a trade name needs its own fictitious-name registration.

permits.name: Florida sales & use tax registration (Florida Business Tax Application / Form DR-1)
permits.notes: Register online through the Florida Business Tax Application (paper Form DR-1 also accepted); allow three business days before checking for your certificate number, then DOR mails a Certificate of Registration and Annual Resale Certificate. Prepared food and drinks are taxed at the 6% state rate plus the county discretionary surtax. The alcohol (DABT) application asks for DOR approval and Miami-Dade's tourist/restaurant tax registration asks for your sales tax number, so file this in week one. Re-register if you move counties, add a location, or change entity.

permits.name: Reemployment (unemployment) tax registration
permits.notes: You become liable once you pay $1,500 or more in wages in a calendar quarter or have at least one employee in 20 weeks of a year, and must register by the end of the month following that quarter. Use the same online Florida Business Tax Application as sales tax. New employers start at 2.7% on the first $7,000 of each employee's wages. Payroll providers need the account number before the first quarterly filing.

permits.name: Workers' compensation insurance (4+ employees, non-construction)
permits.issuing_agency: Licensed carrier (regulated by Florida CFO – Division of Workers' Compensation)
permits.notes: Non-construction employers must carry coverage once they have four or more full- or part-time employees, and corporate officers and LLC members count toward the four. Construction employers (including your build-out contractor) need coverage from the first employee. Premiums are a percentage of payroll, not a government fee. Operating uncovered can trigger a stop-work order that closes the business plus a penalty of twice the premium you should have paid.

permits.name: DBPR Hotels & Restaurants food service plan review (new, converted or remodeled space)
permits.issuing_agency: Florida DBPR – Division of Hotels and Restaurants
permits.notes: Florida restaurants are licensed by the state (DBPR), not the county health department. Plan review is required for a space never licensed by the Division, a space closed more than 18 months, a remodeled space, or a menu or concept change that needs different equipment. It is currently free. Submit a floor plan with labeled equipment and a sample menu. DBPR recommends the combination license + plan review application, which is the fastest route to the licensing inspection.

permits.name: DBPR Public Food Service Establishment license (the Florida restaurant license)
permits.issuing_agency: Florida DBPR – Division of Hotels and Restaurants
permits.notes: Every restaurant, cafe, caterer and hotel food outlet needs this state license before serving the public. You pay a $50 application fee plus an annual fee set by seat count: $262 for 1–49 seats up to $357 for 500+, or $242 if you have no seats. Half-year fees apply if you open six months or less before your district's renewal date. Create a DBPR Online account, apply and pay, then schedule the sanitation and safety licensing inspection, which must pass before opening. City BTRs and the DABT alcohol application ask for this license or its approval.
permits.stall_risk: The licensing inspection can only be scheduled after plan review approval and payment, and missing documents or a failed inspection push the opening date. File the combination application early and walk the space against the approved plan before calling for the inspection.

permits.name: Certified Food Protection Manager (DBPR food manager certification)
permits.issuing_agency: Accredited exam provider (ServSafe, NRFSP, Prometric, StateFoodSafety, etc.) recognized by Florida DBPR
permits.notes: Florida law requires food managers to complete training and pass an accredited certification exam within 30 days of employment. Inspectors ask for proof of certification during inspections. Certify the opening chef or GM before the DBPR licensing inspection so the certificate is on file from day one.

permits.name: DBPR-approved food service employee training (all food staff)
permits.issuing_agency: Florida DBPR – Division of Hotels and Restaurants (approved training programs)
permits.notes: Every food service employee must complete a Division-approved food handler course, generally within 60 days of hire, and repeat it every three years. Use a provider from DBPR's approved training-program list, since third-party providers report completions to DBPR. Operators with an approved in-house program and their own certified manager can train staff themselves. Keep certificates on site for inspections.

permits.name: DABT 2COP license – beer & wine for on-premises consumption
permits.issuing_agency: Florida DBPR – Division of Alcoholic Beverages and Tobacco (DABT)
permits.notes: Non-quota beer & wine license used by restaurants, cafes and wine/beer bars. Sales can be by the drink or in sealed containers. The annual fee is $392 in counties over 100,000 people (Miami-Dade, Broward, Palm Beach, Orange, etc.) and as low as $168 in small counties. The application packet needs local zoning approval, Hotels & Restaurants approval, DOR approval, fingerprints, a sketch of the premises and proof of right of occupancy. A temporary license can be issued while DABT investigates if the application is complete and the temporary fee is paid.
permits.stall_risk: DABT will not accept the application without the city or county zoning sign-off, and alcohol distance-separation rules can block the site. Get the local zoning or alcohol-use approval before you sign the lease.

permits.name: DABT 4COP-SFS Special Food Service Establishment license (full liquor, formerly 'SRX')
permits.issuing_agency: Florida DBPR – Division of Alcoholic Beverages and Tobacco (DABT)
permits.notes: This is the non-quota route to a full bar for larger restaurants, long known as the 'SRX' special restaurant license. DABT's current license guide (updated 2025) requires 2,000 sq ft of service area, equipment to serve 120 people at once, at least 120 physical seats, and 51%+ of food-and-beverage revenue from food and non-alcoholic drinks. The older SRX standard was 2,500 sq ft and 150 seats, so confirm with DABT before designing to the old numbers. The annual fee is $1,820 in large counties. The licensee can't run a package store, must stop alcohol sales when food service ends, and can't move the license to another location.
permits.stall_risk: Seat count and service-area square footage are measured at the DABT inspection, and the 51% food test is audited later. Design the floor plan to clear the minimums with margin and set up POS reporting that separates food from alcohol sales from day one.

permits.name: DABT 4COP quota license – full liquor (bars and smaller restaurants)
permits.issuing_agency: Florida DBPR – Division of Alcoholic Beverages and Tobacco (DABT)
permits.notes: Each county's number of full-liquor quota licenses is capped by population. New ones are released only through DABT's annual drawing ($100 per entry; the 2026 entry window ran Aug 17–Sep 30 for 63 licenses in 30 counties), and winning only gives you the right to apply. Most bars therefore buy an existing quota license on the secondary market, commonly six figures in South Florida, and file a transfer. The annual fee in large counties is $1,820. Hotels with 100+ rooms in counties over 50,000 people should check the non-quota Special Motel/Hotel ('S') license first, and caterers use the 13CT license.
permits.stall_risk: Finding, pricing and escrowing a quota license is usually the longest item for a full-liquor bar. Hire a license broker before signing the lease and make the lease contingent on DABT approving the transfer.

permits.name: DBPR Public Lodging Establishment license (hotel / motel)
permits.issuing_agency: Florida DBPR – Division of Hotels and Restaurants
permits.notes: You pay a $50 application fee plus an annual fee by unit count: $200 for 2–25 units up to $370 for 501+. You must pass a sanitation and safety inspection before opening. Each restaurant or bar inside the hotel needs its own food service license. Hotels whose units are mostly in a building of three or more stories with interior egress need NFPA 13 sprinklers, and buildings of three or more stories must file a balcony inspection certificate every three years.

permits.name: Transient rental (hotel room) sales tax registration
permits.notes: Room rentals of six months or less owe the 6% state sales tax plus the county surtax, and you register on the same Florida Business Tax Application as sales tax. Counties add a local tourist development tax of 3–6%. Some counties administer their own: Miami-Dade collects its convention development tax and food & beverage taxes directly, and Miami Beach, Bal Harbour and Surfside levy their own resort taxes, so you also need the local registration.

permits.name: DBPR Mobile Food Dispensing Vehicle (MFDV) license – statewide food truck license
permits.issuing_agency: Florida DBPR – Division of Hotels and Restaurants
permits.notes: You pay a $50 application fee plus $347 a year ($178.50 for a half year). One license lets the truck operate statewide and covers catering and 1–3 day events. Since July 1, 2020, s. 509.102 F.S. bars cities and counties from requiring any extra food truck license, permit or fee, or banning trucks from their whole jurisdiction, though local location and operating rules still apply. Plan review is needed for a vehicle never licensed, closed more than 18 months, or remodeled. Trucks that are not self-sufficient must use a commissary (form HR 7022) for water and wastewater.
